bibl.title: Beyond confidence: Development of a measure assessing the 5C psychological antecedents of vaccination

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the PSYCHOLOGICAL ANTECEDENTS of vaccination - five of them - and the problem that every existing validated instrument measures mainly ONE of the five
span.quote: Existing validated measures assessing vaccine hesitancy focus primarily on confidence in vaccines and the system that delivers them. However, empirical and theoretical work has stated that complacency (not perceiving diseases as high risk), constraints (structural and psychological barriers), calculation (engagement in extensive information searching), and aspects pertaining to collective responsibility (willingness to protect others) also play a role in explaining vaccination behavior.

span.label: can a short, validated measure be built for all five antecedents, and does it predict vaccination better than the six instruments already in use
span.quote: Study 3 compared the novel scale’s performance with six existing measures of vaccine hesitancy

span.label: the 5C scale in a 15-item and a 5-item version, benchmarked against six existing hesitancy measures across three studies and nearly 2,800 participants
span.quote: As an outcome, a long (15-item) and short (5-item) 5C scale were developed as reliable and valid indicators of confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility.

span.label: method
span.quote: As an outcome, a long (15-item) and short (5-item) 5C scale were developed as reliable and valid indicators of confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility.

span.label: non-vaccination as a behaviour with five separable psychological causes, only one of which - confidence - the field's instruments were built to see
span.quote: Existing validated measures assessing vaccine hesitancy focus primarily on confidence in vaccines and the system that delivers them. However, empirical and theoretical work has stated that complacency (not perceiving diseases as high risk), constraints (structural and psychological barriers), calculation (engagement in extensive information searching), and aspects pertaining to collective responsibility (willingness to protect others) also play a role in explaining vaccination behavior.

span.label: three cross-sectional studies: factor analysis on 1,445 German convenience respondents, a German representative sample of 1,003 testing general against vaccine-specific wording, and a US convenience sample of 350 comparing seven measures head to head
span.term: three cross-sectional studies: factor analysis on 1,445 German convenience respondents, a German representative sample of 1,003 testing general against vaccine-specific wording, and a US convenience sample of 350 comparing seven measures head to head
span.quote: Study 3 compared the novel scale’s performance with six existing measures of vaccine hesitancy

span.label: THE ARGUMENT FOR A NEW SCALE IS AN ARGUMENT ABOUT COVERAGE, NOT ABOUT QUALITY: `existing validated measures ... FOCUS PRIMARILY ON CONFIDENCE in vaccines and the system that delivers them`, while complacency, constraints, calculation and collective responsibility `ALSO PLAY A ROLE`. The instruments were not wrong; they were narrow
span.quote: Existing validated measures assessing vaccine hesitancy focus primarily on confidence in vaccines and the system that delivers them. However, empirical and theoretical work has stated that complacency (not perceiving diseases as high risk), constraints (structural and psychological barriers), calculation (engagement in extensive information searching), and aspects pertaining to collective responsibility (willingness to protect others) also play a role in explaining vaccination behavior.

span.label: and the practical driver is a reporting obligation with no instrument behind it: WHO asks countries to report hesitancy annually in the Joint Reporting Form, and `in 2016, ONLY ABOUT ONE THIRD OF COUNTRIES REPORTED BASED ON THE EVALUATION OF ACTUAL DATA`
span.quote: Such an agreed-upon measure is also needed as WHO asks countries to monitor and report vaccine hesitancy in their annual joint reporting form (JRF) to monitor changes and trends over time and to detect vaccine concerns early [ 9 ]. In 2016, only about one third of countries reported based on the evaluation of actual data, demonstrating the need for a simple but valid measure

span.label: THE VALIDITY EVIDENCE IS OF ONE KIND ONLY, AND THE ABSTRACT SAYS SO: `THE PRESENT STUDIES ARE LIMITED TO THE CONCURRENT VALIDITY OF THE SCALES`. No predictive validation over time, and the outcome in every study is self-reported vaccination
span.quote: The present studies are limited to the concurrent validity of the scales.

span.label: two of the three samples are GERMAN CONVENIENCE SAMPLES and the third is a US convenience sample of 350; only one of the three is representative, and only for age and gender
span.quote: Study 3 compared the novel scale’s performance with six existing measures of vaccine hesitancy

span.label: THE DEFINITION IT QUOTES IS NOT THE ONE ITS SOURCE WROTE. It gives the WHO SAGE definition in quotation marks, cited to macdonald2015, as `refusal of VACCINES despite availability of VACCINE SERVICES` - and macdonald2015 says VACCINATION and VACCINATION SERVICES, twice, identically. The variant appeared in larson2015's Discussion in the same year
span.quote: The first international systematic endeavor was a working group of a WHO advisory body (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization, SAGE), defining vaccine hesitancy as the “delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccine services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence

span.label: and the winning margin is reported as a range across a band of measures rather than a difference: the 5C was `CONSTANTLY AMONG the scales that explained the highest amounts of variance`, 20% to 40%. Among, not above
span.quote: In a comparison of seven measures the 5C scale was constantly among the scales that explained the highest amounts of variance in analyses predicting single vaccinations

span.label: the scale deliberately yields NO total score, so it cannot state how hesitant a sample is - only which determinants predict vaccination
span.quote: As another consequence, using the 5C scale will not lead to a total score providing a sample’s absolute state of hesitancy.

span.label: because hesitancy has no agreed definition, content validity cannot be established against an external criterion, and correlations with psychological constructs are used instead
span.quote: Additionally, lacking a definition of hesitancy makes it difficult to establish external criteria to assess content validity.

span.label: the paper abandons `hesitancy` as its own umbrella term rather than adopting a contested one
span.quote: As there is no agreed upon definition of the phenomenon of “vaccine hesitancy”, in this work we avoid “hesitancy” as a conceptual umbrella for the 5C scale.

span.label: the mapping of existing scales onto the theoretical models rests on the authors' own assumptions, cross-validated by correspondence for only three of them
span.quote: Categorizing of the sub-scales is based on the authors’ assumptions and has been cross-validated in personal communication with the original scales’ authors for PACV, VCS, and VHS.

span.label: MMR uptake in the Study 2 sample was so high that there was little variance left in the outcome, which the paper says may have reduced the predictive power of every scale tested
span.quote: As a limitation, it is important to note that the uptake for MMR was very high in the sample (93.1%), so there was not much variance in the dependent variable.

span.label: the collective responsibility sub-scale collapsed to a single item in Study 2 because the three-item solution was not reliable
span.quote: Unfortunately, the collective responsibility sub-scale resulted in only one item, as the 3-item solution was not reliable.

span.label: one comparison scale was found by an online search and is understood to be still in development, and was included anyway to survey the field
span.quote: The scale was obtained during an online search, to our understanding this is a scale in development.

span.label: the Vaccine Hesitancy Scale items had never been psychometrically validated before, as its own authors note
span.quote: As the authors note, there has never been a psychometric validation since the items were proposed.

span.label: the new scale was run head to head against SIX existing hesitancy measures in one sample, predicting the same outcomes
span.note: eliminates: the objection that a new instrument is being preferred without comparison - this is the head-to-head brotherton2013 said `future research may seek` to do · outcome: held
span.quote: Study 3 compared the novel scale’s performance with six existing measures of vaccine hesitancy

span.label: whether the items must be reworded for each vaccine
span.note: eliminates: the need for vaccine-specific versions - `the new scale provided SIMILAR RESULTS when formulated in a general vs. vaccine-specific way` · outcome: held
span.quote: The new scale provided similar results when formulated in a general vs. vaccine-specific way

span.label: whether the scale predicts vaccination rather than merely correlating with attitudes measured at the same moment
span.note: eliminates: nothing - `THE PRESENT STUDIES ARE LIMITED TO THE CONCURRENT VALIDITY OF THE SCALES`, stated in the abstract · outcome: failed
span.quote: The present studies are limited to the concurrent validity of the scales.

span.label: two attention checks in the MTurk sample, with the analysis re-run excluding those who failed
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that crowd-worker inattention produced the reported structure · outcome: held
span.quote: In order to check the data quality in the MTurk sample we conducted two attention checks [ 86 ].

span.label: randomising the order of the seven measures and of the items inside each measure
span.note: eliminates: order and carry-over effects between the competing scales being compared · outcome: held
span.quote: Then, the seven vaccination measures were assessed in random order and the sequence of the items within each measure was randomized, too.

span.label: assessing social desirability alongside the new collective responsibility sub-scale
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that a scale about protecting others is measuring the wish to appear good · outcome: held
span.quote: Communal orientation and social desirability were assessed as in Study 1 and 2 to validate the new 5C sub-scale collective responsibility and to check for its relation to socially desirable response tendencies.

span.label: powering the sample to detect a correlation as small as r = .2 at 95% power
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that a null relation is an artefact of too few participants · outcome: held
span.quote: Sample size was optimized for detecting small correlations ( r = .2) with at least 95% power [ 62 ].

span.label: vaccine hesitancy
span.quote: The first international systematic endeavor was a working group of a WHO advisory body (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization, SAGE), defining vaccine hesitancy as the “delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccine services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence

span.label: confidence
span.quote: Existing validated measures assessing vaccine hesitancy focus primarily on confidence in vaccines and the system that delivers them. However, empirical and theoretical work has stated that complacency (not perceiving diseases as high risk), constraints (structural and psychological barriers), calculation (engagement in extensive information searching), and aspects pertaining to collective responsibility (willingness to protect others) also play a role in explaining vaccination behavior.

span.label: 5C scale
span.quote: As an outcome, a long (15-item) and short (5-item) 5C scale were developed as reliable and valid indicators of confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility.

span.label: acceptance
span.quote: There is some debate in the literature how we should name the fact that some people do not vaccinate–hesitancy, a lack of confidence or trust, and low acceptance are often used interchangeably

span.label: concurrent validity
span.quote: The present studies are limited to the concurrent validity of the scales.

span.label: 3C model
span.quote: The factors complacency (not perceiving diseases as high risk and vaccination as necessary), convenience (practical barriers) and confidence (lack of trust in safety and effectiveness of vaccines)–referred to as the 3C model–were identified based on experience in various countries [ 16 ] and extensive literature review [ 13 ].

span.label: 4C model
span.quote: Based on literature reviews and theoretical considerations, we extended the 3C model to a 4C model (column 2) by integrating calculation (the individual’s engagement in extensive information searching) as an additional psychological antecedent.

span.label: 5A model
span.quote: The 5A taxonomy for explaining vaccine uptake provides a somewhat different terminology.

span.label: activation
span.quote: The 5A taxonomy adds an additional aspect–activation–which notes the existence of nudges in the environment that may increase vaccination (e.g., reminders [ 14 ]).

span.label: herd immunity
span.quote: Finally, the awareness concept also includes the social benefits of vaccination, i.e., the fact that due to herd immunity most vaccinations also protect unvaccinated individuals [ 27 ].

span.label: Theory of Planned Behavior
span.quote: referring to established theoretical frameworks, such as the Health Belief Model [ 24 ] and the Theory of Planned Behavior [ 23 ].

span.label: convenience
span.quote: convenience: physical availability, affordability and willingness-to-pay, geographical accessibility, ability to understand (language and health literacy) and appeal of immunization service convenience: structural barriers, perceived behavioral control access: ability of individuals to be reached by, or to reach, recommended vaccines affordability: ability of individuals to afford vaccination -- -- -- -- -- -- Constraints complacency: perceived risks of diseases are low; vaccination not seen as necessary complacency: low involvement, low general knowledge, awareness, vaccination not seen as the injunctive norm awareness: knowledge (need for/availability of vaccines) -- -- importance -- -- -- Complacency -- calculation: individuals’ engagement in extensive information search -- -- -- -- -- -- Calculation -- -- activation: degree to which individuals are nudged towards vaccination uptake -- -- -- -- -- -- -- (awareness: social benefits) -- -- -- -- -- -- collective responsibility -- -- compatibility with religious beliefs -- -- -- -- The left part of this table shows that the approaches to understanding vaccine hesitancy and acceptance differ in the number of concepts and the level of specificity with which the concepts are defined.

span.label: THE NAMING PROBLEM, STATED IN THE PAPER'S OWN WORDS: `there is some debate in the literature HOW WE SHOULD NAME the fact that some people do not vaccinate - HESITANCY, A LACK OF CONFIDENCE OR TRUST, AND LOW ACCEPTANCE ARE OFTEN USED INTERCHANGEABLY`. Three names, one phenomenon, and the paper does not choose
span.quote: There is some debate in the literature how we should name the fact that some people do not vaccinate–hesitancy, a lack of confidence or trust, and low acceptance are often used interchangeably

span.label: vaccine hesitancy, AS QUOTED HERE - `delay in acceptance or refusal of VACCINES despite availability of VACCINE SERVICES`. IN QUOTATION MARKS AND CITED TO ITS SOURCE, AND THE SOURCE SAYS `VACCINATION` AND `VACCINATION SERVICES`. Third textual form of one definition, now in a paper by different authors in a different country

Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence

span.label: the 5 Cs - CONFIDENCE, COMPLACENCY, CONSTRAINTS, CALCULATION, COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY. macdonald2015's model was confidence, complacency, CONVENIENCE. Convenience is gone, three terms are new, and THE NAME `the Cs` SURVIVED THE CHANGE OF MEMBERSHIP
span.quote: As an outcome, a long (15-item) and short (5-item) 5C scale were developed as reliable and valid indicators of confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility.

span.quote: In the present contribution, we devise a novel measure to capture relevant predictors of vaccination behavior–the 5C scale, which measures the “psychological antecedents of vaccination” as suggested in a recent review by Brewer and colleagues

span.quote: In the present contribution, we devise a novel measure to capture relevant predictors of vaccination behavior–the 5C scale, which measures the “psychological antecedents of vaccination” as suggested in a recent review by Brewer and colleagues

span.label: critiques → the term `hesitancy` itself, whose behavioural definition is said to absorb access failures and outright refusal alike
span.quote: The term hesitancy has been criticized as its behavioral definition neglects that hesitancy can also be a psychological state of indecision and that any type of non-vaccination is now labeled hesitancy, even though access, system failures or total refusal may be the cause [ 28 ].

span.label: critiques → the term `convenience`, which is said to place responsibility on the individual for what may be a failure of the delivery system
span.quote: Further, the term convenience puts the responsibility of receiving a vaccine to the individual, mixing up social determinants with access.

span.label: builds-on → the SAGE working group definition of vaccine hesitancy
span.quote: The first international systematic endeavor was a working group of a WHO advisory body (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization, SAGE), defining vaccine hesitancy as the “delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccine services.

span.label: critiques → the existing hesitancy measures, which are said to concentrate on confidence and rarely reach the other constructs
span.quote: As can be seen in Table 1 , most existing measures focus primarily on the confidence-related aspects of hesitancy and only occasionally go beyond this major factor (for a detailed description of the scales, see methods sections of Studies 2 and 3).

span.label: vaccine hesitancy —same-as→ acceptance
span.quote: There is some debate in the literature how we should name the fact that some people do not vaccinate–hesitancy, a lack of confidence or trust, and low acceptance are often used interchangeably

span.label: constraints —same-as→ convenience
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — A RENAMING WITH ITS REASON ATTACHED, which is rarer than a renaming. The paper changes the word because the old one assigns blame: `convenience` implies the individual did not prioritise it, when the cause may sit in the delivery system. The 5A model solved the same problem by splitting `access` out instead. Same defect, two different repairs, both recorded on this record.
span.quote: In a similar vein, we propose “constraints” as a synonym for perceived barriers as a new term for convenience.

span.label: the rival taxonomies overlap heavily once aligned - acceptance maps to confidence, access and affordability to convenience, awareness to complacency
span.quote: As is obvious from Table 1 , there is considerable overlap to the categories proposed by the SAGE working group: acceptance resembles the confidence factor (attitude as a potential linkage), access matches convenience (practical barriers), likewise affordability (financial costs; practical and financial barriers are included in the convenience factor), and awareness is comparable to complacency (lack of the perception that the diseases are high risk and that vaccination is necessary).

span.label: calculation, the disposition to search extensively for information, is often POSITIVELY correlated with hesitancy
span.quote: This factor captures the individual motivation of thinking about and questioning vaccination [ 22 ] and is often positively correlated with vaccine hesitancy [ 9 , 25 ].

span.label: a systematic review of influenza vaccine hesitancy found the non-confidence constructs also predict intention and behaviour
span.quote: However, a recent systematic review on influenza vaccine hesitancy has shown that the other constructs proposed in the hesitancy models are also important predictors of vaccination intention and behavior [ 11 ].

span.label: existing instruments run from 4 to 20 items and mostly measure confidence, so a short broad measure is the stated gap
span.quote: In addition, the existing scales are quite lengthy and use between 8 and 20 items to assess different facets of confidence ( Table 1 )–with the exception of the GVCI, which has only 4 items.

span.label: which antecedents predict uptake varies by vaccine - confidence alone for MMR and HPV, all five for influenza - yet a general measure still captures the overall pattern
span.quote: The pattern of significant predictors was more or less independent from the general vs. specific wording: for MMR and HPV vaccine, confidence was the only predictor in both models; for influenza vaccine, all antecedents were significant predictors when measured in a specific way; in the general model, collective responsibility was not significant.

span.label: the one-item-per-sub-scale short version was as valid as the long version, which is what makes field monitoring possible
span.quote: The short version turned out as valid as the long version, which allows the future use of one item per sub-scale (e.g., in field settings or for monitoring) without losing validity.

span.label: the 5C confidence sub-scale overlaps heavily with existing confidence instruments while the other four sub-scales are distinct from them
span.quote: When comparing the 5C scale with existing scales, the results showed that there is considerable overlap with the 5C confidence sub-scale and existing scales that assess confidence (PACV, VCS; see also Table 1 ) and sufficient distinctiveness from the existing scales when looking at the other sub-scales.

span.label: a vaccine-specific wording gave no overall advantage over the general wording
span.quote: Generally, there was no overarching advantage of using a vaccine-specific version.

span.label: compatibility with religious beliefs is measured by one existing index and is covered by NO existing theoretical model, including this paper's own

span.label: the number of new collective-responsibility candidate items written for Study 3
span.quote: As Study 2 revealed that for collective responsibility the available items were not suitable to build a reliable sub-scale, we constructed 11 new candidates, all verbalizing the idea that free-riding (reverse) or ensuring community/herd immunity is a good idea (e.g., “Ensuring community immunity is an important reason for me to get vaccinated.”).

span.label: concurrent validity
span.quote: The present studies are limited to the concurrent validity of the scales.

span.label: the reliability of the rebuilt collective responsibility sub-scale and its correlation with communal orientation
span.quote: The sub-scale’s Cronbach’s α was .71; its correlation with communal orientation was r = -.17, p < .001; for downplaying negative qualities (social desirability) r = -.32, p < .001, and .09, ns, for emphasizing positive qualities.

span.label: the MMR uptake ceiling in the Study 2 sample
span.quote: As a limitation, it is important to note that the uptake for MMR was very high in the sample (93.1%), so there was not much variance in the dependent variable.

span.label: the individual difference the paper substitutes for the 5A environmental category: proneness to nudges against need for thorough processing
span.quote: As we intend to measure individual psychological differences, we suggest assessing the individual proneness to nudges (system 1 processing) vs. a need for thorough information processing (system 2) [ 26 ].

span.label: vaccination behaviour operationalised as a count of recommended vaccines received, with different ranges for adults and children
span.quote: General vaccination behavior was again assessed as the sum of previously received recommended vaccines (yes/no/don’t know; regarding pertussis, tetanus, polio, diphtheria, influenza, measles, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, varicella, pneumococcus, meningococcus C; don’t know was counted as missing value, sum ranging between 0 and 11).
